title: Red Red
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Twice red — the stew from red palm oil, the plantains ripe and fried — with black-eyed peas, smoked fish and a tin of tomato sauce.
longDesc: Red red is Ghana's famous bean stew with fried plantain, and the name is doubly earned: the stew is red from the tomato and the palm oil, and it is served with ripe red-gold plantains. A cup of dried black-eyed peas is quick-boiled two minutes, stood an hour and cooked until tender, about an hour or so. A large onion, half a pound of smoked fish, an eight-ounce tin of tomato sauce and a third of a cup of red palm oil make the stew, which simmers about ten minutes with the salt left until the end because the smoked fish is salty. Plantains fry in a quarter to half an inch of oil.
ingredients: 1 cup black-eyed peas, uncooked — or about 3 cups cooked or frozen
Several nicely ripened plantains, firm not overly ripe
1/2 tsp salt, or to taste — the smoked fish is salty
Chilli to taste — begin with about 1/2 tsp dried
Vegetable oil, for frying the plantain
Ginger, garlic, herbs, powdered shrimp, dry gari, 1-2 tbsp tomato paste
equipment: Second frying pan, for the plantain
steps: Quick-boil the black-eyed peas 2 minutes, then stand 1 hour.
Cook them until tender, about an hour or so.
Add the tomato sauce, palm oil, chilli and smoked fish.
Add the cooked beans and the salt at the end.
Heat the frying oil to about a quarter to half an inch deep.
Fry the plantain slices, turning when they are well-browned on one side.
Serve the stew with the fried plantain alongside.
chefTips: Salt at the end, not the beginning. The smoked fish is salty and you cannot take it back out.
Firm, not overly ripe plantains. Her own specification — they need to hold their shape in the pan and still be sweet.
A quarter to half an inch of oil for the plantain. Shallow frying, not deep.
Turn when well-browned on one side, which is the only frying cue given. Once per side.
A third of a cup of palm oil, and the red of the dish comes as much from the oil as from the tomato.
The quick-boil-and-stand-an-hour is a shortcut for an overnight soak. Then about an hour of real cooking.
A lighter alternative she offers: boiled or roasted plantain instead of fried. It makes a much leaner plate and is a genuine option rather than a compromise.
commonMistakes: Salting before the smoked fish has gone in.
Over-ripe plantains that disintegrate in the pan.
Deep-frying rather than shallow-frying the plantain.
Substituting another oil for red palm oil.
sources: Adapted from "Recipe #85: Ghana's famous 'red-red'", betumiblog.blogspot.com, 14 July 2011. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 12:13 PM'. NO YIELD is printed; the six servings above is editorial.

Ingredients as printed. Items marked here were confirmed on both fetches: 1 cup black-eyed peas, uncooked (or about 3 cups cooked or frozen); 1 large onion, chopped; ~1/2 pound smoked fish; 1 8-ounce can tomato sauce; 1/3 cup red palm oil. THE REST ARE SINGLE-PASS: several nicely ripened plantains (firm, not overly ripe); 1/2 teaspoon salt (or to taste; smoked fish is salty); chili to taste (begin with about 1/2 teaspoon dried); vegetable oil for frying plantain; optional ginger, garlic, herbs, powdered shrimp, dry gari, tomato paste (1-2 tablespoons).

Method, SINGLE-PASS quotes: beans 'cook until tender, about an hour or so', after a quick boil for 2 minutes and a 1 hour stand; stew 'saute for about 10 minutes', leaving the salt until the end; 'After simmering for about 10 minutes'; plantain oil 'to about 1/4 to 1/2 inch', turning 'when they are well-browned on one side'.

THE NAME, as printed: 'the name of an (appropriately) red stew, served with ripe plantains', with the red also referring to 'the (red) palm oil'. So the name is explained twice over by the source. It is 'also delicious when made with aduki (or your choice of) beans.'
A LIGHTER OPTION, from the second fetch: boiled or roasted plantain in place of fried.

AN EARLIER VERSION BY THE SAME AUTHOR, published separately at GHA070 because it differs materially and does not use the name: 'Recipe #18: Bean Stew w/smoked fish', 13 October 2009, byline 'Posted by Fran at 10:45 AM'. THE PHRASE 'RED RED' DOES NOT APPEAR IN IT. Its quantities, TWO-PASS: 1 cup dried cowpeas (washed, soaked and cooked); 1 medium onion; 8-oz can tomato sauce; 1/2 pound smoked fish; about 1/4-1/3 cup palm oil; 1/2 t salt; '1/8 - ? t dried red pepper' — THE QUESTION MARK IS PRINTED; 'Simmer approximately 20 minutes'. Quote: 'it freezes well, it tastes even better the next day'.

THE DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN THE AUTHOR'S TWO VERSIONS, unreconciled: #18 uses 1/4-1/3 cup palm oil and simmers about 20 minutes with no plantain and no 'red red' name; #85 uses 1/3 cup palm oil, simmers about 10 minutes, and adds the fried plantain that makes it red red. Published as two entries.
A THIRD DOCUMENTED RED RED, from a different author and with a much longer cook, is at GHA071.

A NAME THAT COULD NOT BE SOURCED: 'yoo ke gari' appears in NO acceptable source. Red red is the closest published bean-and-gari dish but it CANNOT BE CONFIRMED that they are the same dish. A Wikipedia 'Gari and beans' page exists and was not used, having no named author. A gfw.co.uk red red page showed no byline or date and was excluded.
storage: 4 days refrigerated, 3 months frozen. Fry the plantain fresh.
reheating: Gentle heat. The stew improves overnight.
healthBenefits: Black-eyed peas are high in plant protein, folate, iron and soluble fibre.
Red palm oil supplies provitamin-A carotenoids and vitamin E tocotrienols.
Smoked fish adds omega-3 fats, protein and iodine.
Beans and plantain together give a low-glycaemic, high-fibre plate.
culturalNote: Red red is sold from roadside pans with a mound of fried plantain and a sprinkle of gari, and it is probably the single most-eaten cooked meal in southern Ghana. The doubled name is a good joke about a dish where every element is some shade of red or orange.
